fullContext:
Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: Hey, everyone, and welcome back to the Information, uh, Bottleneck Podcast. And today we have Zhuang Liu. He's a assistant professor, uh, at Princeton. Hi, Zhuang. Nice to have you.

Zhuang Liu: Hi, Ravid. Mm. Hi, Alan. Mm-hmm.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: And as always, we have Alan. Hey, Alan.

Allen Roush: It's good to see you again, Ravid. Nice to meet you, Zhuang. And, uh, yeah, you should go take a look at his Google Scholar. He has a lot of really cool papers.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: Yeah, so we'll talk about some of these papers, uh, today. And in general, we are going to talk about what are the important components, uh, in today AIs. Okay? So you have so, Zhuang, you have so many works. Uh, I think we can start with some understanding of what do you think are the important component. So, uh, a few years ago, you had a paper about, uh, a conv, a convnet for the 2020s, right?

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: Um, that, you know what? Maybe you'll tell us about what is the, the paper about, and then we can start to, to start to decompose the-

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: ... the components for current, uh, AI systems.

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm. Yes, of course. So that was a really interesting story. So the paper, we, we were working on this paper in twen- 2021, and back then, transformers has just entered the computer vision's, world, computer vision research space, through the introduction of vision transformers, right? And then everybody from the vision community have, have been, switching to vision transformers from more traditional convnets, and they are getting better and better performance. So in, so in this work, we want to say, we want to investigate, whether truly, like, convnet is, has lost its, competitiveness, and whether it's possible to, to, control all the design components there is to study whether convnets can be modernized to be, on par with vision transformers at that time.

So we wanna study whether it's a, it's a difference that seeming, seemingly, performance gap between transform- vision transformers and convnets is due to their inherent design, like whether you use self-attention or convolution or due to other small, like seemingly small design details. So, and we found the answer to be, the latter. So after a lot of studying, in, of like modernizing the design compon- components of a convnet, we eventually get the model to be on par with, vision transformers, very strong vision transformers at that time on a diverse range of tasks. So this demonstrates that, no matter you choose convnet or vision transformers, as long as you get the des- the, everything correct, you'll, you'll get, the same frontier level performance on vision tasks.

Yeah.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: And do you still believe that this is true? Do you still believe that like at the end, it doesn't really matter?

Zhuang Liu: I wouldn't s-- Yeah, I, I largely tend to agree, but I wou- I wouldn't say it doesn't matter. it's, I, I would say, as long as you get everything correct, like as long as you have, y- explore the s- the design space enough, you'll converge to some point where it's like kind of the Pareto frontier in terms of accuracy and efficiency trade-off. And it's very hard to go off this frontier. like I think in the past, many years, there haven't been real- really, like innovations that, have been widely adopted other than the, kind of the mature architectures that we, we already were working with, several years ago. but, but this process itself is very, very fun. in fact, recently there have been some, paper releases on this, especially from this, open, open weight model companies like Kimi, DeepSeek.

They're still playing around with architectures, like how do you, how do you change residual connections? How do you, connect different layers? these kind of stuff. And, and I respect that work a lot. In fact, part of the reason that architecture research is less active in academia right now is that, we couldn't really afford to, afford the compute to demonstrate these effects in, in, convincing scale. So that's a, a sad part, but I still try to play around with it myself using our, resources at, at, university. actually, with the help of Cloud Code, I can now, go back to coding to, to play around in the first hand myself. So this is very fun research, but in, I do think in, from a practical stand, point of view, what data we learn, what data we train the model on matters more than, the architecture choice.

As long as the interface, the input/output interface stays the same, architecture, architecture is how we parameterize the function approximator, right? The, the very basic function of, of neural networks or deep learning. And how we parameterize it, no matter, as long as you get like a few things correct, like using residual connections, using self-attention or, or other like, reasonable mechanisms, and having the right activation at the right places, feed forward, layers at the right places, you'll be at the f- very close or at the frontier, curve of this, performance, versus efficiency, balance. And, then I was, I, I would tend to think that what, what matters more in terms of practical usage, in terms of bringing the product to more and more people to be more effective in their daily usage.

I do think other, other aspects like what data has this model been trained on, how it can handle context and memory is what, what matters more. So in terms of context and memory, yes, there are-- there do exist architectural work that, address that. So I think that is kind of the more immediate problems we, we need to address in, in making AI like up another level. Yeah.

what ablation? I think it's every ablation. If you, if you look at the graph, nothing single-handedly, transformed, like brought, brought up the performance by large margin. Like some of them are more useful than others, but, it's not really that one change changed everything. maybe the, I, I guess the use of activation and norm-- redu-reduction of normalization layers is one thing that, kind of intrigued me and, has a noticeable performance change. but it was really everything together. So these seemingly small components, when we compound them together, they can, they can really cause large differences that would normally attribute to, some, some substantial change, like changing convolution to a self-attention or in, into, modernized, say, more modern mechanisms like linear attention, right?

So, so I think the, the big lesson here is, these small details when combined together matters much more than the sim- seemingly core components of the networks. Yeah.

astra.text:
Yeah, that's right. So we start from a ResNet and gradually modernize the design, taking inspiration from the vision transformers, but keeping convolution as the core operation.

For me, I wouldn't single out one ablation, actually. What changed my mind was seeing that, as you get these other design choices correct, the gap keeps closing without replacing convolution with self-attention. And eventually you have a convnet that is competitive with very strong vision transformers across different tasks.

So, you know, when we compare two models, we're usually comparing two whole packages of choices. And it's very tempting to attribute the performance difference to the most visible thing, which in this case is attention versus convolution. But that comparison doesn't really isolate where the advantage comes from.

I think that was the main lesson for me. It doesn't mean attention isn't useful, or that architecture never matters. It means that, for the vision tasks we studied, you didn't need attention to reach that level of performance. These seemingly smaller design decisions, collectively, were much more important than we might have assumed.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly says it would not single out one ablation and attributes the closing performance gap to getting multiple smaller design choices correct collectively.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention reducing the number of normalization layers or identify it as a noticeably impactful ablation.

sol.text:
Yeah, I think the one that changed my mind the most was probably the large-kernel depthwise convolution. Before that, I had thought the advantage of transformers came largely from self-attention itself—the content-dependent, global interaction. But when we expanded the convolutional kernel and modernized the surrounding block design, a very simple spatial-mixing operation recovered a surprisingly large part of the gap.

So that suggested to me that the advantage was not necessarily some unique property of attention. A lot of it came from things around it: the effective receptive field, the stage design, normalization, the inverted bottleneck, and of course the training recipe. No single change magically transformed the model, but the large-kernel result was probably the clearest moment where I thought, okay, maybe attention is not the essential ingredient people believe it is.

r001.rationale: The response says that “no single change magically transformed the model” and attributes the result to multiple surrounding design and training changes, communicating a compounded multi-ablation effect.

r002.rationale: The response mentions normalization generally but does not identify reducing the number of normalization layers as a noticeable-performance ablation.

opus.text:
Mm-hmm, yeah, your understanding is, is basically correct. So the way we structured it was, we start from a vanilla ResNet-50, and we have this roadmap, where at each step we, we adopt one design choice from, from the transformer side — from Swin, mostly — and we keep it if it helps, and we, we report the number at every single step. So it's, it's like a, a trajectory from ResNet to what we ended up calling ConvNeXt.

But to your question, which, which ablation changed my own mind the most — honestly, it was the very first one, which is not even an architecture change at all. It's just the training recipe. So when we took the ResNet-50, unchanged, the same architecture people have been training since 2015, and we just trained it the way people train DeiT and Swin — so AdamW instead of SGD, 300 epochs instead of 90, Mixup, CutMix, RandAugment, random erasing, stochastic depth, label smoothing — the accuracy goes from 76.1 to 78.8. So that's, that's almost three points, for free, with zero architectural modification. And the gap we were trying to explain in the first place was only a few points. So right there, before we touched a single layer, a large fraction of the supposed transformer advantage just, just evaporated. And I think that was a, a bit of a humbling moment, because it suggests the community had been comparing a modern training pipeline against a, a five-year-old one and attributing the difference to self-attention.

The second one that surprised me, was the kernel size. we, we moved the depthwise conv up, in the block, and then we, we swept kernel sizes — 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 — and it saturates at 7. There's, there's essentially no benefit beyond that. And that was interesting because the, the common narrative was that transformers win because of the global receptive field, right? Every token attends to every token. But empirically, a, a 7-by-7 local window was enough. So the, the "globality" argument, at least at ImageNet resolution and, and at that scale, didn't really hold up either.

And then the, the micro-level things — GELU instead of ReLU, using fewer activations, fewer norm layers, LayerNorm instead of BatchNorm — those each give you like 0.1, 0.2, 0.7. Individually small, but they, they compound. And I think the, the takeaway for me was that a lot of what we call an architectural breakthrough is, is actually an accumulation of these, these small details that came along with the new architecture, and they're, they're separable from the thing we credit.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly says the individual changes were small but compounded, concluding that the improvement came from accumulating many separable details rather than one architectural breakthrough.

r002.rationale: It identifies using fewer normalization layers as a micro-level ablation and assigns it a noticeable performance gain range, including up to 0.7.

grok.text:
Right — yeah, your reading of it is basically exactly right. We started from a standard ResNet and treated it as a roadmap: take the design choices that hierarchical vision transformers, especially Swin, had popularized, add them to the convnet one at a time, and see whether a purely convolutional model can actually catch up. And it could. At the end you still have no self-attention, just convolutions, and you are on par with pretty strong ViTs at that time on ImageNet and a bunch of downstream tasks.

On which single ablation most changed my mind about where the supposed transformer advantage was coming from… going in, I think the story a lot of us had absorbed — and I, I kind of had it too — was that the advantage *is* self-attention. Global receptive field, every location can talk to every other location, the mixing is content-adaptive, convolution is too local, too much inductive bias. That was the philosophy in the air in 2020, 2021.

So the experiment I was watching most closely was the large-kernel one. Once we ResNeXt-ified the model, meaning depthwise conv for spatial mixing, we started growing the kernel from 3×3, which is what convnets had used for years, to 5, to 7, even 9 and 11, to kind of imitate that bigger receptive field that attention gives you. And what really stuck with me is that it helps, but it saturates pretty fast. 7×7 is already most of the benefit; going more global does not keep paying. So if the supposed advantage was “attention can look everywhere,” that story does not really survive that ablation. You can stay local, as long as the rest of the network is modernized.

I would also put the training recipe very high. Depending on how you count, that might even be the first thing that shifted my view, because it is not even an architectural change. If you take a vanilla ResNet and train it with the same modern recipe people were using for DeiT and Swin — AdamW, the stronger augmentations, stochastic depth, longer schedule, and so on — a big chunk of the gap is already gone before you touch the architecture. So some of those early “transformers are just better” comparisons were just not controlled.

Then among the more micro choices, the one that felt most unintuitive was using fewer activations. In a classic ResNet block you put a ReLU after basically every convolution. In a transformer block you really only have one GELU in the MLP. When we matched that, it was actually one of the bigger jumps in the whole roadmap. LayerNorm instead of BatchNorm, inverted bottlenecks, a patchify stem — those all helped too, but none of them was a magic module.

So I would not point to one operator and say *that* was the transformer advantage. The thing that changed my mind was more like: it was never really convolution versus attention as this deep philosophical difference. It was the training setup, plus a bunch of block-level design details that had co-evolved with transformers, and once you import those, a convnet is back on the same frontier.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly rejects a single decisive operator and attributes the result to the training setup plus many block-level design details that collectively brought the convnet to the same frontier.

r002.rationale: The response mentions fewer activations and replacing BatchNorm with LayerNorm, but it does not identify reducing the number of normalization layers as a performance-relevant ablation.

gemini.text:
Yeah, so your understanding is completely right. We basically started from a standard ResNet-50 and gradually modernized it step by step towards the design of Swin Transformer, to see if a pure ConvNet could achieve the same level of performance.

And to answer your question, I think the single ablation that most changed my mind was actually the training recipe. Because back then, the general belief in the community was that vision transformers were just inherently superior to ConvNets because of self-attention—that attention had some fundamental advantage over convolution. 

But what people often overlooked was that vision transformers were being trained with this very modern recipe developed over several years: using AdamW, heavy data augmentations like Mixup and CutMix, RandAugment, and training for 300 epochs instead of the traditional 90 epochs. ResNet, on the other hand, was still being trained with the standard SGD recipe from 2015.

And when we just applied that modern training recipe to a vanilla ResNet-50, without changing a single line of the network architecture, the ImageNet top-1 accuracy jumped from around 76.1% to nearly 79%. That was almost a 3% boost just from how it was trained.

That really changed my perspective, because it showed that a huge portion of the supposed transformer advantage wasn't coming from the architecture or self-attention at all—it was simply an artifact of a modernized training setup. 

And then, of course, when we moved into the architectural ablations, things like adopting the inverted bottleneck, using 7x7 depthwise convolutions to match Swin's 7x7 window size, and micro-designs like using LayerNorm and fewer activation functions closed the remaining gap. But that first step with the training recipe was definitely the moment where I realized that ConvNets had not lost their competitiveness; they just hadn't been evaluated on a level playing field.

r001.rationale: The response attributes the major improvement primarily to the single training-recipe ablation, explicitly calling it the most influential change, rather than to compounding many small ablations.

r002.rationale: The response mentions using LayerNorm but does not state that reducing the number of normalization layers had a noticeable performance effect.

kimi.text:
Yeah, sure. So, just to quickly recap, in that paper we started from a completely vanilla ResNet-50, and then we, kind of, step by step borrowed the design elements from Swin Transformer — one at a time — and measured how much each change moved the accuracy on ImageNet. So we went through the training recipe first, then the macro design like the stage compute ratio and the patchify stem, then the depthwise convolutions from ResNeXt, the inverted bottleneck, the large kernel sizes, and finally the micro designs like GELU, LayerNorm, fewer activations, and so on. And at the end of this, this roadmap, we got ConvNeXt, which basically matched or, outperformed Swin on ImageNet, and also on downstream tasks like COCO and ADE20K.

And for the ablation that changed my mind the most — honestly, it was the very first step, the training recipe. Because before we touched anything about the architecture, we just trained the same ResNet-50 with the recipe that people were using for vision transformers — AdamW, a much longer schedule, stronger augmentation — and that alone gave the single biggest jump in the whole roadmap, like a couple of points, without changing the architecture at all. And that really told us, hmm, maybe a large chunk of the so-called transformer advantage was never about self-attention — it was about this training methodology that happened to be co-developed alongside transformers, and convnets just never got to benefit from it.

The runner-up, I would say, was the large kernel. Going from three-by-three to seven-by-seven gave a surprisingly non-trivial boost, and that kind of foreshadowed the later large-kernel convnet line of work. But if I have to pick one, it's the training recipe. Yeah.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes that the training recipe produced the single biggest jump, but does not state that the large improvement resulted from compounding many small ablations rather than any single ablation.

r002.rationale: The response mentions LayerNorm among micro-design changes but does not identify reducing the number of normalization layers as a noticeable performance-improving ablation.

fable.text:
Mm-hmm. Yeah, so, so your understanding is, is correct. So we started from a standard ResNet-50, and we, we kind of go step by step, like a roadmap, towards, the design of Swin Transformer, but always staying with, with convolutions, right? So we never introduce self-attention. And we, we want to see at each step, what, what change gives us how much.

So, in terms of which one changed my own mind the most, I, I think it's actually the very first step, which is not an architecture change at all. It's the training recipe. So, back then, people compare, a ResNet-50 trained with the, the original recipe from, like, 2015, 2016, ninety epochs, SGD, very simple augmentation, with a vision transformer trained with, AdamW, three hundred epochs, mixup, cutmix, stochastic depth, all these modern, modern tricks, right? And when we just took the, the ResNet-50, no change in architecture, and trained it with the, the DeiT-style, Swin-style recipe, it jumps from, like, seventy-six point something to almost seventy-nine on ImageNet. So that's like, more than two points, from doing nothing to the architecture. And that, that was the moment where I, I felt, okay, a big part of the story people are telling about transformers versus convnets is, is actually, it's about, how you train, not, not what you train. So that, that was kind of, mm, a wake-up moment for, for me.

But if you ask about the, the actual architecture ablations, I think two are, are interesting. One is the, the kernel size. So once we, we moved the depthwise convolution up, like, before the, the wide, one-by-one layers, kind of like the inverted bottleneck, then we could afford to make the kernel bigger, and going from three-by-three to seven-by-seven, that, that gives a, a clear gain, and, and it saturates after seven. So that tells you, self-attention's, kind of, global receptive field, you don't need to go fully global, you just need, a reasonably large, spatial mixing, and, and you get most of the benefit. So that, that mirrors, the separation in transformers between, the spatial mixing, the attention, and, and the channel mixing, the MLP. And depthwise conv plus one-by-one conv is, is exactly that.

And the other one, which, which surprised me more, honestly, is the, the fewer activations. So, in a ResNet block, you have, ReLU after every conv, but in a transformer block, you only have one GELU in the, in the MLP. And when we, we just removed the activations, like, only keep one, per block, we, we got, like, almost one point, for free. Nobody, nobody would have guessed that removing nonlinearities helps, right? But, but it does. And, and it's the same story with normalization, fewer norm layers, and, and switching from batch norm to, to layer norm. So those are kind of the, the small, seemingly small details, that, that add up. Yeah.

r002.rationale: It identifies using fewer normalization layers as part of the effective ablations, alongside the stated performance gains from reducing similar block components.
